Big Tech Facing Data Center Backlash
 
Plus, Mercedes gives Its cars an AI upgrade and AI agents as CMOs
 
 
MARTINA TUATY FOR WSJ
 

Americans are sizing up their finances after Democrats’ blowout victories in the midterm elections Tuesday.

 

The results point to a new financial and tax-policy agenda that could take flight if the Democrats win the presidency in 2028, as President Trump is expected to block major changes while he is still in the White House.

 

For individuals, that would mean two years to maximize tax breaks and prepare portfolios for policy shifts ahead.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

 
 
 

Planning & Investing

 

How the Data Center Backlash Could Play Into the Hands of Big Tech

 

With Democrats taking not just the U.S. House and Senate, but also the governorships of states such as Texas, Ohio and Georgia, investors are now contemplating more roadblocks emerging for the construction of data centers.

 
 
 

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Developments in the Middle East conflict are likely to be the main influence on the Bank of England’s interest rate decisions over the coming months, Moneyfarm’s Richard Flax says in a note. The BOE raised interest rates to 4.0% on Thursday in a widely expected move. The BOE also acknowledged that the economy has been more resilient than expected, which raises the risk of high inflation as energy costs remain elevated. “As the bank now forecasts inflation hitting 5% next year, it feels like the tightening cycle has once again commenced,” Flax says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

 

The U.S. midterm results overall appear favorable for Canada’s economy as the prospect of tariff relief and lower oil prices have increased, which could also strengthen the case for the data center build-out in Canada, KPMG Canada’s Ali Jaffery reckons. Still, the economist sees some risk and says it is hard to have high conviction early on. “The new Congress doesn’t take office until January, and a lot can change in short order.” Jaffery notes the U.S. administration’s preferred strategy so far has been “de-escalation by escalation” so it is unclear how it will react now that its legislative back is against the wall. He adds that Canadian tariffs featured in a few key races but wonders if Democrats can and will use their leverage to now remove those levies. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)
